title: Rock and sand (Matthew 7:24–27)
hook: the wise build on rock by doing these words, not just hearing them

segments.voice: Yesterday, karpos: fruit, what a life actually grows. Your line was know it by its fruit.

You've seen the footage. A storm rolls in, the river rises, and a house that looked fine yesterday slides sideways into the water. Before the storm, you couldn't have told which houses would stand. Same paint, same windows, same view. The difference was underneath, where nobody looks. For almost three chapters Jesus has been talking on this hillside: blessed are the poor in spirit, love your enemies, the Lord's Prayer, the birds, the lilies, the narrow gate. Now he ends the whole sermon with a story about two builders and one storm.
screen: `THE HOUSE SLIDES INTO THE RIVER.` → `SAME PAINT, SAME WINDOWS.` → `TWO BUILDERS, ONE STORM.`

segments.voice: It starts like this, in the King James Bible: "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock." Two verbs: hear, and do. Then the storm: "And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock." Then the second builder, and almost word for word, the same storm. Jesus doesn't promise the wise builder skips it. Both houses get hit. The only difference is what's underneath, and that the second one "heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not." It isn't the listener against the one who skipped the sermon. Both heard every word. One did it, and one didn't. The ending is blunt: "and it fell: and great was the fall of it." In that part of the world, there are dry riverbeds that sit flat and sandy most of the year, easy to build on. Then a winter storm comes, and they fill with a rushing flood in an hour. Building on the sand wasn't stupid. It was easy. Rock takes digging. The Greek word for rock is petra, and listeners who know the Gospels will hear an echo later, when Jesus gives Simon the nickname Peter, the rock. The point is simple and hard. Nobody builds a house by listening to a podcast about houses. The sermon only holds if it's done.
screen: `HEAR, AND DO.` · `THE SAME STORM FOR BOTH.` · `SAND IS EASY; ROCK TAKES DIGGING.` · `PETRA: ROCK.`

segments.voice: Walk back through the sermon in your mind and choose just one thing to do: give something in secret, take the plank out first, watch a bird instead of worrying, or do for someone what you'd want done for you. Picture exactly when and where you'll do it. That's one stone laid on rock.
Petra, the Greek word for rock, bedrock, the same word behind Peter's name. Two builders heard the same words and faced the same storm. One did what he heard.
Your line: build on rock. Rock takes digging, but it holds through the storm. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Christians treat this parable as the key to the whole Sermon on the Mount, and children in many churches learn it as a song about the wise man who built his house upon the rock.

guess: rock: solid bedrock you can build on
sand: the loose ground of a dry riverbed
a small stone you can hold in your hand

match.prompt: the two builders — tap the pairs.

myth: the wise builder's house missed the storm
the rain, floods and winds are the same for both. the ground underneath is different.
the foolish builder never heard the sermon

fork.setup: you've heard the whole sermon. the storm is coming. what makes your house stand?
options: a good view and strong paint.
fork.reveal: "whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them" builds on rock. hearing alone is sand.

original.note: Greek: rock, bedrock; the same word echoes when Simon is called Peter.

trapdoor: what you thought: good people don't get hit by storms.
what it means: storms come for everyone; what holds is having done the words, not just heard them.
what a scholar hears: the sermon's closing parable, hear-and-do; dry riverbeds that flood in winter; and petra, echoed in Peter's name.

notes: Audit (10% sample): fixed a garbled sentence ('Not hearing versus not hearing'); 'word for word' softened to 'almost word for word', since the Greek verbs for the wind beating the house differ (7:25 prospiptō, 7:27 proskoptō).
Dry riverbeds (wadis) that flood in winter as the background to the 'sand': common commentary suggestion, not stated in the text. Confirm the wording.
The Peter/petra echo: Matthew 16:18 uses petros and petra; the script says 'an echo'. Confirm.
